newsitem.title: UK: UK to raise public sector pay by average 3.3 pct.
newsitem.headline: UK to raise public sector pay by average 3.3 pct.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major's government, just three months away from an election, agreed on Thursday to give more than a million nurses, teachers and other state workers a 3.3 percent pay rise.

But to keep spending in check, Major said the increase would be paid in two stages, saving a total of 263 million pounds ($431 million) and bringing it down below the rate of inflation -- forecast at 2.5 percent.
A senior official said the award, which will cost a total of 805 million pounds, "strikes a balance between the interests of the taxpayer and the interests of staff".
But unions criticised the government's refusal to pay the increase -- recommended by independent pay review bodies -- in one go.
Major also came under fire from opposition parties, which accused him of being unfair to nurses and teachers while being generous to high-earning judges and senior military officers.

Labour's economics spokesman, Gordon Brown, attacked the decision to keep the general increase for nurses, teachers, doctors and rank-and-file soldiers just 3.3 percent, while the pay of top judges was allowed to rise sevent percent.

Brown confirmed Labour, hot favourite to win the election, would also phase in the awards for doctors, nurses, teachers and the armed forces but would scrap rises of up to six percent for 5,000 judges, military chiefs and top civil servants.
"We know we will inherit a difficult position which means that we can make no additional promises," Brown said.
But Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, who has insisted pay rises must be met from existing spending plans, defended the awards.
"It's a sensible, fair approach to pay which good public sevices and good companies have to adopt in this low inflation world where we're all getting a bit better off," Clarke said.
